claim: N-acyl amino acids are a family of bioactive lipids with pleiotropic physiologic functions, including in energy homeostasis.
source: The N-acyl amino acids are a family of bioactive lipids with pleiotropic physiologic functions, including in energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about N-acyl amino acids that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: PM20D1 (peptidase M20 domain containing 1) is an extracellular mammalian N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase that regulates endogenous N-acyl amino acid levels.
source: Their endogenous levels are regulated by an extracellular mammalian N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase called PM20D1 (peptidase M20 domain containing 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work establishing PM20D1's role.

claim: FAAH is a second intracellular N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase.
source: Using an activity-guided biochemical approach, we report the molecular identification of fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) as a second intracellular N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data presented throughout the results section.

claim: FAAH exhibits a more restricted substrate scope compared to PM20D1 in vitro.
source: In vitro, FAAH exhibits a more restricted substrate scope compared to PM20D1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing substrate specificity of FAAH and PM20D1 shown in Figure 3.

claim: Genetic ablation or selective pharmacological inhibition of FAAH bidirectionally dysregulates intracellular, but not circulating, N-acyl amino acids in mice.
source: In mice, genetic ablation or selective pharmacological inhibition of FAAH bidirectionally dysregulates intracellular, but not circulating, N-acyl amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from FAAH-KO mice and PF-3845 treatment shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dual blockade of both PM20D1 and FAAH reveals a dramatic and non-additive biochemical engagement of these two enzymatic pathways.
source: Dual blockade of both PM20D1 and FAAH reveals a dramatic and non-additive biochemical engagement of these two enzymatic pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PM20D1-KO mice treated with PF-3845 shown in Figure 5.

claim: Individual members of the mammalian N-acyl amino acids have been previously implicated in appetite, nociception, vasoregulation, and bone health.
source: Individual members of the mammalian N-acyl amino acids have been previously implicated in appetite, nociception, vasoregulation, and bone health (Milman et al., 2006; Mostyn et al., 2019; Parmar and Ho, 2010; Smoum et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Certain N-acyl amino acids stimulate oxidative metabolism via mitochondrial uncoupling.
source: We have recently identified a new role for certain N-acyl amino acids in stimulating oxidative metabolism via mitochondrial uncoupling (Long et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Thermogenic N-acyl amino acids are characterized by medium-chain fatty acyl chains and neutral amino acid head groups.
source: These thermogenic N-acyl amino acids are characterized by medium-chain fatty acyl chains and neutral amino acid head groups, chemical features that are present in a subset of family members including N-acyl phenylalanines, N-acyl leucines, N-acyl glycines, and N-acyl serines (Keipert et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work characterizing these molecules.

claim: Administration of thermogenic N-acyl amino acids to mice rendered obese by feeding a high-fat diet increases energy expenditure, reduces adiposity, and improves glucose homeostasis.
source: Consequently, administration of these N-acyl amino acids to mice rendered obese by feeding a high-fat diet increases energy expenditure, reduces adiposity, and improves glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous citations about thermogenic N-acyl amino acids.

claim: PM20D1 is a classically secreted enzyme present in the circulation in both mice and humans.
source: PM20D1 is a classically secreted enzyme present in the circulation in both mice and humans (Schwenk et al., 2017; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recombinant PM20D1 functions as a bidirectional N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase in vitro, catalyzing the biosynthesis of N-acyl amino acids from free fatty acids and free amino acids, as well as the reverse hydrolysis reaction.
source: In vitro, recombinant PM20D1 functions as a bidirectional N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase, catalyzing the biosynthesis of N-acyl amino acids from free fatty acids and free amino acids, as well as the reverse hydrolysis reaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work on PM20D1.

claim: Overexpression of PM20D1 in mice drives the biosynthesis of circulating N-acyl amino acids in vivo.
source: Overexpression of PM20D1 in mice, achieved by adeno-associated viral vectors, drives the biosynthesis of circulating N-acyl amino acids in vivo.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work with PM20D1.

claim: Mice with PM20D1 overexpression have increased energy expenditure and reduced adiposity on high-fat diet.
source: These mice consequently have increased energy expenditure and reduced adiposity on high-fat diet.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about PM20D1 overexpression effects.

claim: Global ablation of PM20D1 leads to a complex, bidirectional dysregulation of N-acyl amino acid levels and metabolic dysfunction characterized by glucose intolerance and decreased insulin sensitivity.
source: Conversely, global ablation of PM20D1 leads to a complex, bidirectional dysregulation of N-acyl amino acid levels and metabolic dysfunction characterized by glucose intolerance and decreased insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on previous work with PM20D1-KO mice.

claim: Polymorphisms within and near the human PM20D1 gene are linked to body mass index.
source: Polymorphisms within and near the human PM20D1 gene are linked to body mass index (Benson et al., 2019; Bycroft et al., 2018), providing powerful genetic evidence that PM20D1 may also regulate human obesity and metabolic disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: PM20D1 may regulate human obesity and metabolic disorders.
source: Polymorphisms within and near the human PM20D1 gene are linked to body mass index (Benson et al., 2019; Bycroft et al., 2018), providing powerful genetic evidence that PM20D1 may also regulate human obesity and metabolic disorders.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on genetic associations.

claim: Other mammalian enzymes beyond PM20D1 are likely to contribute to N-acyl amino acid metabolism.
source: Beyond PM20D1, other mammalian enzymes are also likely to contribute to N-acyl amino acid metabolism, especially considering the large and structurally diverse nature of this lipid family (Aneetha et al., 2009; Bradshaw et al., 2009; Cohen et al., 2017; Waluk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inference based on the diversity of the lipid family and citations to related work.

claim: In wild-type mice, robust hydrolysis of C20:4-Phe was observed in eight of the ten tissues tested, with activities in the range of ~0.01 nmol/min/mg (lung) to 1.0 nmol/min/mg (liver).
source: In wild-type mice, robust hydrolysis of C20:4-Phe was observed in eight of the ten tissues tested, with activities in the range of ~0.01 nmol/min/mg (lung) to 1.0 nmol/min/mg (liver).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In PM20D1-KO tissues, the hydrolysis of C20:4-Phe was completely abolished (>99% reduction in each tissue).
source: In PM20D1-KO tissues, the hydrolysis of C20:4-Phe was completely abolished (>99% reduction in each tissue), establishing that PM20D1 is the only enzyme responsible for C20:4-Phe hydrolysis activity (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: PM20D1 is the only enzyme responsible for C20:4-Phe hydrolysis activity.
source: In PM20D1-KO tissues, the hydrolysis of C20:4-Phe was completely abolished (>99% reduction in each tissue), establishing that PM20D1 is the only enzyme responsible for C20:4-Phe hydrolysis activity (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is inferred from the complete loss of activity in PM20D1-KO tissues.

claim: Using C20:4-Gly as a substrate, both brain and liver from PM20D1-KO mice maintained a robust second hydrolysis activity.
source: By contrast, using C20:4-Gly as a substrate, both brain and liver from PM20D1-KO mice maintained a robust second hydrolysis activity (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The second PM20D1-independent activity accounted for 70% and 11% of the total C20:4-Gly hydrolysis in brain and liver, respectively.
source: The second PM20D1-independent activity accounted for 70% and 11% of the total C20:4-Gly hydrolysis in brain and liver, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data comparing WT and PM20D1-KO tissues.

claim: The residual activity in PM20D1-KO liver was higher (0.10 nmol/min/mg) than that observed in the knockout brain tissue (0.03 nmol/min/mg).
source: In absolute terms, the residual activity in PM20D1-KO liver was higher (0.10 nmol/min/mg) than that observed in the knockout brain tissue (0.03 nmol/min/mg).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from tissue lysates.

claim: The residual activity is only present for C20:4-Gly but not C20:4-Phe, suggesting that this second enzyme might exhibit selectivity for regulating subsets of lipid species within the N-acyl amino acid family.
source: That this residual activity is only present for C20:4-Gly but not C20:4-Phe suggested that this second enzyme might exhibit selectivity for regulating subsets of lipid species within the N-acyl amino acid family.
evidence: This is inference and speculation based on the differential substrate activity observed.

claim: PM20D1 is one of five members of the mammalian M20 peptidase family.
source: PM20D1 is one of five members of the mammalian M20 peptidase family, all of which exhibit peptide bond hydrolysis and condensation activity on a variety of small molecule substrates such as N-acetyl amino acids (Sass et al., 2006), N-lactoyl amino acids (Jansen et al., 2015), and other dipeptides (Kim et al., 2019; Teufel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the M20 peptidase family supported by citations.

claim: All mammalian M20 peptidases exhibit peptide bond hydrolysis and condensation activity on a variety of small molecule substrates such as N-acetyl amino acids, N-lactoyl amino acids, and other dipeptides.
source: PM20D1 is one of five members of the mammalian M20 peptidase family, all of which exhibit peptide bond hydrolysis and condensation activity on a variety of small molecule substrates such as N-acetyl amino acids (Sass et al., 2006), N-lactoyl amino acids (Jansen et al., 2015), and other dipeptides (Kim et al., 2019; Teufel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on M20 peptidases.

claim: Only PM20D1-transfected cells exhibited robust conversion of C20:4-Gly to arachidonic acid among the mammalian M20 peptidases tested.
source: Only PM20D1-transfected cells exhibited robust conversion of C20:4-Gly to arachidonic acid (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Other mammalian M20 peptidases are excluded as candidate enzymes for catalyzing the residual N-acyl amino acid hydrolysis activity in PM20D1-KO tissues.
source: These data therefore exclude any other mammalian M20 peptidases as a candidate enzyme for catalyzing the residual N-acyl amino acid hydrolysis activity in PM20D1-KO tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of activity in other M20 peptidase transfected cells.

claim: The vast majority of the C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity from PM20D1-KO livers remained in the membrane fraction after differential centrifugation at 100,000 x g.
source: Compared to the whole liver, the vast majority of the hydrolysis activity remained in the membrane fraction (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The responsible enzyme for the residual activity contains a transmembrane domain or is otherwise tightly associated with cellular membranes.
source: This observation suggested that the responsible enzyme contains a transmembrane domain or is otherwise tightly associated with cellular membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the membrane localization of the activity.

claim: Pre-treatment of PM20D1-KO liver membrane lysates with MAFP completely abolished the residual C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity.
source: Remarkably, pre-treatment of PM20D1-KO liver membrane lysates with MAFP completely abolished the residual C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity, whereas the other broad-spectrum enzyme inhibitors were entirely without effect (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The residual hydrolysis activity is due to a serine hydrolase that is sensitive to MAFP inhibition.
source: These data strongly suggest that the residual hydrolysis activity is due to a serine hydrolase that is sensitive to MAFP inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective inhibition by MAFP, a serine hydrolase inhibitor.

claim: The mammalian serine hydrolases are a large family of more than 250 enzymes.
source: The mammalian serine hydrolases are a large family of more than 250 enzymes (Bachovchin and Cravatt, 2012; Long and Cravatt, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Serine hydrolases are characterized by a serine nucleophile that catalyzes hydrolytic reactions via a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate.
source: These hydrolases are characterized by a serine nucleophile that catalyzes hydrolytic reactions via a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about serine hydrolases.

claim: FAAH contains an N-terminal transmembrane domain and internal intramembrane region.
source: First, FAAH contains an N-terminal transmembrane domain and internal intramembrane region, consistent with the observation that the residual hydrolysis activity is localized to liver membranes rather than to the cytosolic fraction (Patricelli et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work on FAAH.

claim: FAAH has been shown to regulate several classes of bioactive fatty acid amides, including the N-acyl ethanolamines and N-acyl taurines.
source: Second, FAAH has been shown to regulate several classes of bioactive fatty acid amides, including the N-acyl ethanolamines and N-acyl taurines, both of which share considerable structural similarity with N-acyl amino acids (Grevengoed et al., 2019; Saghatelian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on FAAH substrates.

claim: FAAH exhibits highest expression in brain and liver in mice.
source: Last, FAAH exhibits highest expression in brain and liver in mice, the two anatomical locations where we observe the highest residual N-acyl amino acid hydrolysis activity in PM20D1-KO mice (Long et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous expression data.

claim: Pre-treatment of PM20D1-KO liver membrane lysates with PF-3845 (10 µM) completely blocked the residual hydrolysis activity.
source: Pre-treatment of PM20D1-KO liver membrane lysates with PF-3845 (10 µM) completely blocked the residual hydrolysis activity exactly as was previously observed with MAFP (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: A distinct serine hydrolase inhibitor that does not inhibit FAAH (WWL70, 10 µM) had no effect on the residual C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity.
source: By contrast, a distinct serine hydrolase inhibitor that does not inhibit FAAH (WWL70, 10 µM) had no effect on the residual C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different inhibitors.

claim: A dose–response curve established an EC50 of 290 nM for PF-3845 on the residual C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity.
source: A dose–response curve established an EC50 of 290 nM for PF-3845, a concentration consistent with the previously reported potency of this compound towards FAAH (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: FAAH is the enzyme responsible for the residual N-acyl amino acid hydrolysis activity in PM20D1-KO tissues.
source: Taken together, these data establish FAAH as the enzyme responsible for the residual N-acyl amino acid hydrolysis activity in PM20D1-KO tissues.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: PM20D1 was most closely related to ACY1 (24% identity) and shared little identity with FAAH (11%).
source: PM20D1 was most closely related to ACY1 (24% identity) and shared little identity with FAAH (11%).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: FAAH was localized entirely intracellularly, consistent with its previously described localization as an ER-associated transmembrane enzyme.
source: As expected, FAAH was localized entirely intracellularly, consistent with its previously described localization as an ER-associated transmembrane enzyme, whereas PM20D1 protein was largely found in the conditioned media, consistent with its known annotation as a classically secreted enzyme (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and citations to previous work.

claim: PM20D1 protein was largely found in the conditioned media, consistent with its known annotation as a classically secreted enzyme.
source: As expected, FAAH was localized entirely intracellularly, consistent with its previously described localization as an ER-associated transmembrane enzyme, whereas PM20D1 protein was largely found in the conditioned media, consistent with its known annotation as a classically secreted enzyme (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and established knowledge about PM20D1.

claim: FAAH-transfected cells showed robust hydrolysis activity for four N-acyl amino acids tested: C18:1-Gly, C18:1-Ser, C20:4-Gly, and C20:4-Ser.
source: FAAH-transfected cells showed robust hydrolysis activity for four N-acyl amino acids tested: C18:1-Gly, C18:1-Ser, C20:4-Gly, and C20:4-Ser (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A strong preference was observed for C20:4-Ser over the other three N-acyl amino acid substrates (~1.5 nmol/min/mg for FAAH hydrolysis of C20:4-Ser versus 0.05–0.15 nmol/min/mg for any of the other substrates).
source: A strong preference was observed for C20:4-Ser over the other three N-acyl amino acid substrates (~1.5 nmol/min/mg for FAAH hydrolysis of C20:4-Ser versus 0.05–0.15 nmol/min/mg for any of the other substrates), at least under these in vitro conditions.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of enzyme activity.

claim: FAAH catalyzed the condensation of arachidonic acid with Gly and Ser, but not Phe.
source: In the N-acyl amino acid synthase direction, FAAH also catalyzed the condensation of arachidonic acid with Gly and Ser, but not Phe (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: PM20D1 exhibited robust hydrolysis activity across nearly all members of the N-acyl amino acid substrate panel over mock-transfected background.
source: By contrast, robust hydrolysis activity was observed for PM20D1 across nearly all members of this N-acyl amino acid substrate panel over mock-transfected background (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: PM20D1 efficiently catalyzed the condensation of arachidonic acid with all three Gly, Ser, and Phe amino acids.
source: PM20D1 also efficiently catalyzed the condensation of arachidonic acid with all three Gly, Ser, and Phe amino acids (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: FAAH showed robust hydrolysis activity with anandamide as a substrate (0.5 nmol/min/mg) and lower but similar activities with C20:4-NAT and C20:4-Gly (0.04 and 0.02 nmol/min/mg, respectively).
source: As expected, FAAH showed robust hydrolysis activity with anandamide as a substrate (0.5 nmol/min/mg) and lower but similar activities with C20:4-NAT and C20:4-Gly (0.04 and 0.02 nmol/min/mg, respectively, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: PM20D1 exhibited robust hydrolysis activity only on C20:4-Gly (0.6 nmol/min/mg) and was unable to hydrolyze either anandamide or C20:4-NAT.
source: Conversely, PM20D1 exhibited robust hydrolysis activity only on C20:4-Gly (0.6 nmol/min/mg) and was unable to hydrolyze either anandamide or C20:4-NAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: C20:4-NAT was not a direct inhibitor for PM20D1.
source: We also determined that C20:4-NAT was not a direct inhibitor for PM20D1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Recombinant FAAH is an N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase in vitro.
source: Taken together, these data establish that recombinant FAAH is an N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing both synthesis and hydrolysis activities.

claim: The PM20D1–FAAH pair is an example of convergence in enzymatic activity despite divergence in primary sequence.
source: Our findings also underscore the PM20D1–FAAH pair as an example of convergence in enzymatic activity despite divergence in primary sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence alignment and functional data.

claim: 26 and 14 N-acyl amino acid species were detected in liver and blood, respectively.
source: In these experiments, we were able to detect 26 and 14 N-acyl amino acid species in liver and blood, respectively (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on LC-QQQ mass spectrometry measurements.

claim: C20:4-Glu was elevated by 2.1-fold across all three conditions of FAAH blockade in liver.
source: Those changes that were statistically significant across all three conditions of FAAH blockade were elevations in C20:4-Glu (by 2.1-fold) and decreases in C20:4-Gly (by 70%).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from FAAH-KO and PF-3845 treated mice.

claim: C20:4-Gly was decreased by 70% across all three conditions of FAAH blockade in liver.
source: Those changes that were statistically significant across all three conditions of FAAH blockade were elevations in C20:4-Glu (by 2.1-fold) and decreases in C20:4-Gly (by 70%).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from FAAH-KO and PF-3845 treated mice.

claim: No N-acyl amino acids were significantly changed over controls across all three experiments in the blood.
source: In the blood, no N-acyl amino acids were significantly changed over controls across all three experiments (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PM20D1 activity is not altered in FAAH-KO plasma.
source: We confirmed that PM20D1 activity is not altered in FAAH-KO plasma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hepatic N-acyl amino acids levels were similar to N-acyl ethanolamine and N-acyl taurines in wild-type mice by abundance.
source: By abundance, hepatic N-acyl amino acids levels were similar to N-acyl ethanolamine and N-acyl taurines in wild-type mice (Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from liver extracts.

claim: FAAH is a bidirectional regulator of a subset of intracellular, but not extracellular, N-acyl amino acids.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that FAAH is a bidirectional regulator of a subset of intracellular, but not extracellular, N-acyl amino acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on liver versus blood N-acyl amino acids.

claim: Following PF-3845 treatment in PM20D1-KO mice, the residual hepatic C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity was entirely abolished.
source: Following PF-3845 treatment in PM20D1-KO mice, the residual hepatic C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activity was entirely abolished (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: PM20D1 and FAAH are the only two C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activities in liver, at least under the assay conditions used.
source: These data establish that PM20D1 and FAAH are the only two C20:4-Gly hydrolysis activities in liver, at least under the assay conditions used here, and further validate our previous in vitro studies (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is inferred from the complete loss of activity upon dual blockade.

claim: Complete ablation of N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase activities did not uniformly change N-acyl amino acids in a positive or negative direction.
source: Surprisingly, complete ablation of N-acyl amino acid synthase/hydrolase activities did not uniformly change N-acyl amino acids in a positive or negative direction.
evidence: This is based on the bidirectional changes observed in Figure 5b.

claim: Dual inhibition of PM20D1 and FAAH uncovered a remarkable cooperativity of these two enzymatic pathways in the regulation of N-acyl amino acids.
source: Instead, dual inhibition of PM20D1 and FAAH uncovered a remarkable cooperativity of these two enzymatic pathways in the regulation of N-acyl amino acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-additive effects observed upon dual blockade.

claim: Individual regulation by PM20D1 or FAAH were not predictive of those N-acyl amino acid species that were regulated by both enzymatic pathways together or even the directionality of change.
source: In general, individual regulation by PM20D1 or FAAH were not predictive of those N-acyl amino acid species that were regulated by both enzymatic pathways together or even the directionality of change.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing single versus dual blockade effects.

claim: Hepatic N-acyl serines were largely unaltered by individual blockade of either FAAH or PM20D1 alone.
source: For instance, hepatic N-acyl serines were largely unaltered by individual blockade of either FAAH or PM20D1 alone (Figure 4a and Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 4a and 5b.

claim: Following dual blockade of both enzymes, C18:1-Ser and C20:4-Ser were dramatically accumulated by 13-fold and 26-fold, respectively.
source: Following dual blockade of both enzymes, C18:1-Ser and C20:4-Ser were dramatically accumulated by 13-fold and 26-fold, respectively (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: C18:1-Gly was reduced in PM20D1-KO livers and unaltered by FAAH blockade, but accumulated to 8-fold over controls when both enzymes were inhibited.
source: For instance, C18:1-Gly was reduced in PM20D1-KO livers and unaltered by FAAH blockade, but nevertheless accumulated to 8-fold over controls when both enzymes were inhibited.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing different conditions.

claim: The PM20D1–FAAH pair is an example of enzymatic convergence, despite largely unrelated primary amino acid sequences.
source: Our data uncover the PM20D1–FAAH pair as an example of enzymatic convergence, despite largely unrelated primary amino acid sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence and functional data presented.

claim: Enzymatic and spatial division of labor is a mechanism for the control of subsets of a diverse thermogenic lipid family.
source: More generally, these findings underscore enzymatic and spatial division of labor as a mechanism for the control of subsets of a diverse thermogenic lipid family.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the overall findings.

claim: FAAH is best recognized for its role in endocannabinoid signaling via hydrolysis of the cannabinoid receptor agonist anandamide (N-arachidonoyl-ethanolamine).
source: FAAH is best recognized for its role in endocannabinoid signaling via hydrolysis of the cannabinoid receptor agonist anandamide (N-arachidonoyl-ethanolamine) (Cravatt et al., 1996; Cravatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FAAH supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate pain and inflammation.
source: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate pain and inflammation (Ahn et al., 2009; Cravatt et al., 2001), obesity and metabolic homeostasis (Brown et al., 2012; Touriño et al., 2010), and anxiety and depression (Gobbi et al., 2005; Kathuria et al., 2003), amongst many others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate obesity and metabolic homeostasis.
source: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate pain and inflammation (Ahn et al., 2009; Cravatt et al., 2001), obesity and metabolic homeostasis (Brown et al., 2012; Touriño et al., 2010), and anxiety and depression (Gobbi et al., 2005; Kathuria et al., 2003), amongst many others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate anxiety and depression.
source: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of FAAH has been shown to regulate pain and inflammation (Ahn et al., 2009; Cravatt et al., 2001), obesity and metabolic homeostasis (Brown et al., 2012; Touriño et al., 2010), and anxiety and depression (Gobbi et al., 2005; Kathuria et al., 2003), amongst many others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Polymorphisms in the FAAH gene have provided human genetic evidence for disease associations.
source: Polymorphisms in the FAAH gene have also provided human genetic evidence for these disease associations (Sipe et al., 2002; Sipe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: FAAH phenotypes are classically associated with anandamide elevation and activation of the cannabinoid receptors upon FAAH inhibition or genetic deletion.
source: These phenotypes are classically associated with anandamide elevation and activation of the cannabinoid receptors upon FAAH inhibition or genetic deletion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FAAH's mechanism of action.

claim: Beyond the endocannabinoid system, FAAH also regulates several other classes of bioactive lipids including other N-acyl ethanolamines, N-acyl taurines, and N-acyl amino acids.
source: However, beyond the endocannabinoid system, FAAH also regulates several other classes of bioactive lipids including other N-acyl ethanolamines, N-acyl taurines, and now, N-acyl amino acids.
evidence: This is based on previous work and the current findings.

claim: FAAH-regulated N-acyl amino acids may contribute to some of the observed phenotypes associated with FAAH.
source: We propose that FAAH-regulated N-acyl amino acids may also contribute to some of these observed phenotypes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Complete ablation of all C20:4-Gly synthase/hydrolase activities via dual blockade of both PM20D1 and FAAH was not sufficient to elevate or deplete all endogenous N-acyl amino acids globally.
source: Our data reveal that complete ablation of all C20:4-Gly synthase/hydrolase activities via dual blockade of both PM20D1 and FAAH was not sufficient to elevate or deplete all endogenous N-acyl amino acids globally.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from dual blockade experiments.

claim: Extensive and non-additive interactions were observed between PM20D1 and FAAH in the regulation of specific subsets of N-acyl amino acids.
source: Instead, we observed extensive and non-additive interactions between these two enzymatic pathways in the regulation of specific subsets of N-acyl amino acids.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from dual blockade experiments.

claim: Non-additive interactions between PM20D1 and FAAH could not be predicted by in vitro substrate specificity or even individual N-acyl amino acid regulation.
source: In general, these non-additive interactions could not be predicted by in vitro substrate specificity or even individual N-acyl amino acid regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: This type of cooperativity has not been previously described for any biochemical pathway.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this type of cooperativity has not been previously described for any biochemical pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Additional biochemical pathways beyond PM20D1 and FAAH contribute to regulating the endogenous levels of the N-acyl amino acid lipid family.
source: Last, our findings suggest that additional biochemical pathways beyond PM20D1 and FAAH contribute to regulating the endogenous levels of this lipid family.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete changes observed with dual blockade.

claim: Potential candidate pathways for additional N-acyl amino acid regulation include additional amidase enzymes on other N-acyl amino acid substrates, enzymes that catalyze the conjugation of fatty acid CoAs with amino acids, or non-mammalian sources.

claim: N-acyl amino acids are structurally closely related to other bioactive fatty acid amides including the endogenous cannabinoid receptor agonist anandamide and the N-acyl-homoserine lactone family of bacterial quorum-sensing molecules.
source: Structurally, N-acyl amino acids are closely related to the other bioactive fatty acid amides including the endogenous cannabinoid receptor agonist anandamide (N-arachidonoylethanolamine) and the N-acyl-homoserine lactone family of bacterial quorum-sensing molecules (Devane et al., 1992; Parsek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
